sections.title: Otto Joseph Krause — WWII B-17 navigator
sections.summary: Otto Joseph Krause (20 May 1922 – 6 May 1999; SSDI last residence Rochester, MI 48307) of Detroit served as a navigator with the 91st Bomb Group, 324th Bomb Squadron, Eighth Air Force, based at RAF Bassingbourn. He flew mostly on B-17 Mah Ideel (43-37993 DF-N) with Lt. William Laws’ crew, earned the Air Medal with oak leaf clusters (orders Oct–Dec 1944; advanced 2LT → 1LT), and finished as a First Lieutenant. American Air Museum narrative (details from grandson Chris Krause): on 6 Jan 1945 over the Rhine, flying near Balaban’s B-17 Little Miss Mischief when that ship was hit by flak; Krause directed the damaged bomber to an airfield at Merville, France, where it landed safely for repairs. American Air Museum lists death as 15 Apr 1999 (secondary); SSDI extract gives 6 May 1999 — prefer SSDI until an obituary is found. He married Geraldine Staub around 1945. Postwar job and burial still open.

sections.title: Lucia Kokx — Rotterdam journal (1939–1940)
sections.summary: Tim’s maternal grandmother Lucia Kokx (b. 15 Aug 1928; birthday confirmed from her own journal) wrote these recollections of Rotterdam from summer 1939 through the German bombing of 14 May 1940. Text below is transcribed word for word from the family copy as provided; spelling and wording are preserved. The provided transcript ends mid-sentence.
highlights: Author: Lucia Kokx (Tim Symons’s mother’s mother)
Birthday in journal: August 15; turning 11 in 1939 → birth 15 Aug 1928
Setting: Rotterdam; vacation cabin near Hoek van Holland
Family in journal: mom, dad (postman), grandpa (lived with them after grandma died), younger sister Nel (~10 in May 1940), younger brother Jerry (~6 in May 1940)
Bombing of Rotterdam: 14 May 1940 (also grandpa’s birthday in the journal)
Transcript status: ends mid-sentence as received — more pages welcome

verbatimEntries.title: Rotterdam, July 1939
paragraphs: I was skipping home from school. Our last day, the whole month of August off. I was happy because my parents, for the first time, rented a cabin for the two whole weeks. We have been there before, but only one week. It was right by the ocean and I was Really looking forward to that. Then I had a birthday coming up. August 15. 11 years old, that sounded a lot more than 10. There was one dark note. We heard the grown-ups talking about bad times, a war was coming. In Spain, they were fighting and there were Jewish people rounded up in Germany. But today, I was thinking about our vacation. There were six of our us going, my mom and dad, then there was my grandpa, he lived with us after my grandma died. Then there was my younger sister and brother and me. Mother was already packing things when I got home. We still had a couple of days. But there was a lot to pack.

Finally, the day came, first to the railroad station, then with the train to Hoek van Holland. First from there we had to walk plus or -1 hour with all our baggage. And there we were, our little house for the next two weeks. That first week was beautiful. the weather was perfect. Every day we walked to the beach. We swam and my Dad fished, we picked flowers. Small yellow ones they smelled so good. But everyday on the radio there were those gloomy broadcasts. The adults were nervously talking about war. But holland was a neutral country. That could not happen. The last war we stayed neutral (ww1) but in our second week things started to happen. All the young men had to report for active duty in the service. My dad was a postman and he got ordered back to Rotterdam. We did stay the rest of that week with my mom and grandpa, but it was not the same. School started again in Leptenber. I liked school and saw all my friends again. But things were

Fast changing in Europe. Germany had invaded several countries in the east including Poland. Warchan was bombed and Jews were rounded up. That winter in 1939-1940 was tense. We, as children, had a very normal winter except for bits and pieces of conversation from the adults. It was a cold winter, but finely spring came. We could play outside again. Jump rope, marbles, stilts, hop skotch. Then, May 10 the Germans had invaded Holland. Children had to stay home from school. My dad went to work as usually. We heard airplanes going over our house and the sirens went off. The sound wailing up and down for danger and one tone of everything was safe again. The radio was constantly warning to heed the sirens. There were rumors of Germans parachuting behind the lines of Duch soldiers. Then came May 14 my grandpas birthday. The morning started the same as those last 5 days. Warnings on the radio, my dad went to work. We needed a few

Things from the corner store. So my mother gave me a bag and some money and off I went, only to the corner, not even a block, come right back, she said. I just had paid and got my stuff and the sirens went of again. We heard for of airplanes. The lady from the store said, go home fast! I ran home and found my mother in panick. They (the Germans) were bombing Rotterdam, down town where my dad was. We heard the explosions. The radio station was still on the air telling people “safe” places to go. There were shelters, but the closest to us was 2-3 blocks away. They said, if you live upstairs, go sit on the stairway. So we all sat on the stairs, I was still clutching the bag with the few things from the store, Mom had put her bill fold in there too. We were scarred stiff. We heard the bombs go over with a wishing sound and then we waited for the explosion. And than it happened.

The wisheling was real loud and the explosion was there at ones. Everything turned dark, people on top of the stairs started to shout, out! Out! We stumbled down it was dark and hard to breed. It was 1 pm. We finally made it outside, the front door was gone , now we had to find each other. When we were all together again. We started to run  for the shelter. The dust lifted some and we saw the that the bomb had hit right across the street from our house. Later we found out that duch people had died there. But for now we were on our way to the shelter, but before we got there we were led into a bakery 2 blocks away. It was full of people. For the first time we had a good look at each other. Mom and my little brother, Jerry 6 years old were fine, my sister nel 10 years old had a cut on her head and was bleeding. I had some cut on my hands. All from flying glass. My grandpa was complaining of pain everywere. He sat on the bottom of the stairs and when every body was trying

sections.title: Crosier brothers — Civil War (Charlotte / Carmel)
sections.summary: Ann’s 3×-great-grandfather Charles Crosier (1838 Sullivan, OH – 1917 Charlotte, MI) and his older brother Stephen P. Crosier (1827 Somerset, VT – 1891 Charlotte) are both marked Civil War veterans in the Maple Hill Cemetery index, Charlotte. Stephen P. is confirmed on the roster of Company H, 12th Michigan Infantry, home Carmel, age 37 — the same company that includes George H. Carmoney of Florence (very likely the Carmoney brothers-in-law connection; see Carmoney sisters section). The 12th Michigan left the state in March 1862 and fought at Shiloh (6–7 Apr 1862) in Peabody’s Brigade, Prentiss’ Division; the regiment later served at Vicksburg and in Arkansas and mustered out in 1866. Charles is listed among Sullivan Township (Ashland Co., OH) Civil War volunteers and appears as “Crozier, Charles” on the Company H, 42nd Ohio Volunteer Infantry roster raised in Ashland County (Camp Chase, Nov 1861; mustered out Dec 1864) — a strong match for the Sullivan-born Charles who married Mary Carmoney in Eaton County on 18 Jan 1865, weeks after that muster-out, but a pension/service-file name match would lock the unit. Charles appears again among Charlotte 3rd Ward Civil War veterans in the 1894 Michigan state census.

sections.title: Carmoney sisters married Crosier brothers
sections.summary: Two daughters of John Henry Carmoney and Catherine Bair married two sons of Stephen Park Crosier and Minerva Lucy Howard. Sarah Ann Carmoney (11 Feb 1835 OH – 28 Jan 1911 Charlotte) married Stephen P. Crosier on 4 Jul 1854 in Eaton County. Her younger sister Mary M. Carmoney (9 Mar 1844 Mercer Co., OH – 13 May 1932 Charlotte) married Charles Crosier on 18 Jan 1865 in Eaton County — Ann’s direct line. Both couples settled in Charlotte; Maple Hill holds Crosier/Carmoney stones including Mary M., Sarah A., Stephen P., Freddie, Ada, Halbert, and an infant. Catherine Carmoney is also indexed at Maple Hill. The Ohio→Michigan Carmoney move and the Crosier Vermont→New York→Ohio→Michigan trail (Halifax/Somerset VT → Bainbridge NY → Sullivan OH → Charlotte MI) are the family’s mid-19th-century migration story.

sections.title: Solomon Lozon — sapper details & Order of Foresters
sections.summary: Beyond the basic enlistment already documented: Solomon Alex Lozon (b. 6 Nov 1891 Wallaceburg) was a single labourer on his father’s R.R. #2 Becher/Wallaceburg farm when he attested 26 Feb 1918 at London, ON, to the 1st Western Ontario Regiment (sapper #3131895). Physical description from the file: 5′3″, dark complexion, brown eyes, black hair, small scar on the right wrist; he carried a CEF crest tattoo reading “S. A. Lozon.” He was insured with the Independent Order of Foresters. He embarked 10 May 1918 on S.S. Runio, reached England 24 May, went to the CE pool at Seaford and on to France (Aug–Sep 1918), and returned via Southampton March 1919; medical notes mention prior typhoid (fully recovered, no disability). Brother Peter Dulphy Lozon (#3134471), a single farmer, attested 9 Jul 1918 listing mother Mary Lozon of R.R. #2 Wallaceburg as next of kin (not father) — suggesting Adolphus may already have been dead or absent by mid-1918 (speculative timing; Solomon’s Feb 1918 paper still named father Adolphus). Peter’s enlistment was cancelled/discharged in the demobilization wave (discharged 25 Jan 1919) without the same overseas story.

sections.title: Lauzon / Maillet — French Kent County roots
sections.summary: Adolphus Lozon’s parents Alexandre Lauzon (~1827) and Magdeleine Maillet (b. 11 Apr 1826) married in the St. Pierre / Raleigh–Tilbury East French Catholic corridor of Kent County, Ontario. Trees of Ancestry give the marriage as 1 Jun 1842 at St. Peter Tilbury; MesAieux / YourFolks indexes the same couple as Alexandre Lauson × Magdeleine Maillet in 1846 at Raleigh, ON — treat the year as unresolved between sources until a parish image is pulled. The Lozon/Lauzon spelling shift is normal in this border French community (Wallaceburg, Dover, Tilbury, Grande Pointe). A related Wallaceburg marriage (David Luzon, son of “Alex Luzon and Adeline Myers,” 1879) shows the same parental names anglicized (Myers ≈ Maillet), reinforcing that Adolphus’s generation sat inside a dense French-Ontarian kinship network rather than an isolated English farm family. Do not confuse this Alexandre (~1827) with the better-documented Alexandre Lauzon (1814–1893) of Sandwich/Grande Pointe who married Marie Catherine Martin — a different man in the same surname cluster.

sections.title: Altz family — Rochester roots & Joseph’s millwright story
sections.summary: Norman Altz appears in the 1948 Rochester (Avon Twp.) street directory alongside other residents at the 1421 address cluster — placing Dolores’s parents in Rochester when she was a teenager. Son Joseph Edward Altz (28 Nov 1951 Rochester – 23 Sep 2025 Lapeer), Dolores’s youngest brother, worked 20+ years as a millwright at American Axle in Detroit, later at Pontiac Truck and Bus and Bosch (Lake Orion). He collected Pontiac Fieros and model locomotives, volunteered at Holy Cross Youth Center (Saginaw) and Lapeer Hospital, and was buried from St. Lawrence Catholic Church, Utica. His 2025 obituary reconfirms parents Norman & Rena Altz and sisters including Dolores Crosier. Public trees still do not name Norman’s or Rena La Pan’s parents — that generation remains open.
